evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The KCC2 C-terminal antibody recovered peptides from both isoforms of KCC2.
source: While the KCC2 C-terminal antibody recovered peptides from both isoforms of KCC2, the N-terminal KCC2b-specific antibody did not recover any KCC2a isoform-specific peptides, indicating the specificity of the antibodies used, and the success of KCC2-immunoenrichment in our AP-assays.
evidence: This is based on the mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: The N-terminal KCC2b-specific antibody did not recover any KCC2a isoform-specific peptides.
source: While the KCC2 C-terminal antibody recovered peptides from both isoforms of KCC2, the N-terminal KCC2b-specific antibody did not recover any KCC2a isoform-specific peptides, indicating the specificity of the antibodies used, and the success of KCC2-immunoenrichment in our AP-assays.
evidence: This is based on the mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: 150 putative KCC2 partners were established after filtering and eliminating spurious interactors.
source: By applying these filtering criteria and processes, we established a total list of 150 putative KCC2 partners in our present LC-MS assay (Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on the data filtering and analysis process described in the methods.

claim: More than half of the KCC2 interactors were exclusively enriched in KCC2-APs from the mature brain (85 proteins, ~57% overlap).
source: More than half of these KCC2 interactors were exclusively enriched in KCC2-APs from the mature brain (85 proteins,~57% overlap), while approximately one-third (41 proteins,~27% overlap) were identified across both the developing and mature brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the mass spectrometry data across developmental stages.

claim: Approximately one-third of KCC2 interactors (41 proteins, ~27% overlap) were identified across both the developing and mature brain.
source: More than half of these KCC2 interactors were exclusively enriched in KCC2-APs from the mature brain (85 proteins,~57% overlap), while approximately one-third (41 proteins,~27% overlap) were identified across both the developing and mature brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the mass spectrometry data across developmental stages.

claim: Only 24 proteins (~16% overlap) were exclusively enriched in the developing brain.
source: Only relatively small percentages were exclusively enriched in the developing brain (24 proteins,~16% overlap).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the mass spectrometry data across developmental stages.

claim: The 150 putative KCC2 partners were segregated into high-confidence (platinum, gold), moderate-confidence (silver), or lower confidence (bronze) putative KCC2-interactors.
source: Next, we segregated the 150 putative KCC2 partners into high-confidence (platinum, gold), moderate-confidence (silver), or lower confidence (bronze) putative KCC2-interactors (Figure 3, Table 1 and Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This describes the classification scheme used for the interactors.

claim: Platinum KCC2-partners are proteins enriched in a minimum of two out of three replicates, show 5+ fold spectral enrichment, and a MaxP SAINT score ≥0.89.
source: Platinum KCC2-partners are those proteins enriched in a minimum of two out of three replicates, show 5 + fold spectral enrichment, and a MaxP SAINT score ≥0.89.
evidence: This defines the criteria for platinum classification.

claim: Gold KCC2-partners are proteins enriched in only one replicate with normalized spectral count enrichments ≥ 5 and a MaxP SAINT score ≥0.89.
source: Gold KCC2-partners were those proteins enriched in only one replicate with normalized spectral count enrichments ≥ 5 and a MaxP SAINT score ≥0.89.
evidence: This defines the criteria for gold classification.

claim: Silver KCC2-partners are proteins with normalized spectral count enrichments between 3 and 5, and a MaxP score between 0.7 and 0.89.
source: Silver KCC2-partners were those with normalized spectral count enrichments between 3 and 5, and a MaxP score between 0.7 and 0.89.
evidence: This defines the criteria for silver classification.

claim: 31 proteins that have been previously established as KCC2-physical/functional partners but were not identified in the present LC-MS assay were added to the interactome.
source: Lastly, we added 31 proteins that have been previously established as KCC2-physical/functional partners but were not identified in our present LC-MS assay (Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This describes the inclusion of previously known interactors in the comprehensive interactome.

claim: The proposed KCC2 interactome consists of 181 members (150 proteins identified in the present screen plus 31 previously established partners).
source: The proteins identified in the present screen (150) and the proteins previously established as key KCC2 physical/functional partners (31), together constitutes the 181 members of the proposed KCC2 interactome.
evidence: This is the total count of proteins in the comprehensive KCC2 interactome.

claim: ~43% of proteins in the KCC2 interactome (77/181) were exclusively enriched at excitatory synapses.
source: Interactome mapping revealed that ~43% of proteins in the KCC2 interactome (77/181) were exclusively enriched at excitatory synapses, while only ~2% of proteins (4/181) were exclusively enriched at inhibitory synapses (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is based on mapping the interactome to known synaptic proteomes.

claim: Only ~2% of proteins in the KCC2 interactome (4/181) were exclusively enriched at inhibitory synapses.
source: Interactome mapping revealed that ~43% of proteins in the KCC2 interactome (77/181) were exclusively enriched at excitatory synapses, while only ~2% of proteins (4/181) were exclusively enriched at inhibitory synapses (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is based on mapping the interactome to known synaptic proteomes.

claim: ~15% of proteins in the KCC2 interactome (30/181) were mapped to both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: However, ~15% proteins (30/181) were mapped to both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, whereas ~39% proteins (70/181) did not map to either synapses.
evidence: This is based on mapping the interactome to known synaptic proteomes.

claim: ~39% of proteins in the KCC2 interactome (70/181) did not map to either excitatory or inhibitory synapses.
source: However, ~15% proteins (30/181) were mapped to both excitatory and inhibitory synapses, whereas ~39% proteins (70/181) did not map to either synapses.
evidence: This is based on mapping the interactome to known synaptic proteomes.

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) revealed that KCC2 partners segregate into three broad categories: ion homeostasis, dendritic cytoskeleton rearrangement, and receptor trafficking.
source: Performing this IPA analysis revealed that KCC2 partners segregate into multiple cellular and molecular functional nodes, which we then combined into three broad categories that collectively had high p values: ion homeostasis, dendritic cytoskeleton rearrangement, and receptor trafficking (Figure 4c–e; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on the IPA analysis of the interactome data.

claim: The receptor trafficking network has a clustering coefficient of 0.63 and an average of ~4.4 neighbors.
source: The third category, receptor trafficking, has a denser network (clustering coefficient of 0.63 and an average of ~4.4 neighbors) in comparison to the other networks, suggesting a tight link between KCC2 and proteins in this node.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of the interactome data.

claim: The dense receptor trafficking network suggests a tight link between KCC2 and proteins in this node.
source: The third category, receptor trafficking, has a denser network (clustering coefficient of 0.63 and an average of ~4.4 neighbors) in comparison to the other networks, suggesting a tight link between KCC2 and proteins in this node.
evidence: This is an inference based on the network analysis.

claim: Novel putative-KCC2 partners in the receptor trafficking node include PACSIN1, SNAP25, RAB11FIP5, CSNK2A1, DNM1 and AP2B1.
source: Notably, this analysis revealed multiple novel putative-KCC2 partners, including PACSIN1, SNAP25, RAB11FIP5, CSNK2A1, DNM1 and AP2B1.
evidence: This is based on the IPA analysis identifying these proteins in the receptor trafficking category.

claim: All novel putative interactors in the receptor trafficking node have established functions in membrane recycling and/or trafficking of glutamate receptor subunits.
source: All these novel putative interactors have established functions in membrane recycling and/or trafficking of glutamate receptor subunits (Carroll et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2002; Vandenberghe et al., 2005; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2006; Selak et al., 2009; Sanz-Clemente et al., 2010; Anggono et al., 2013; Bacaj et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on these proteins.

claim: SLC12A5 mRNA is expressed with several members of the receptor trafficking node in the hippocampus.
source: We observed that SLC12A5 mRNA is expressed with several members of the receptor trafficking node in the hippocampus (Figure 5a), amygdala, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on transcriptomic analysis of human brain RNAseq data.

claim: SLC12A5 mRNA is expressed with several members of the receptor trafficking node in the amygdala, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex.
source: We observed that SLC12A5 mRNA is expressed with several members of the receptor trafficking node in the hippocampus (Figure 5a), amygdala, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on transcriptomic analysis of human brain RNAseq data.

claim: PACSIN1 was immunoprecipitated with an anti-KCC2b antibody, but not with control IgY antibodies.
source: We found that PACSIN1 was immunoprecipitated with an anti-KCC2b antibody, but not with control IgY antibodies (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5b.

claim: KCC2 was immunoprecipitated with a PACSIN1 antibody, confirming the existence of a KCC2-complex with PACSIN1 in vivo.
source: Using a previously well-validated PACSIN1 antibody (Anggono et al., 2013), we confirmed this interaction in the reverse direction, indicating the existence of a KCC2-complex with PACSIN1 in vivo (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on reverse co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The expression profiles of KCC2 and PACSIN1 are temporally aligned in the mouse brain.
source: Consistent with our ability to co-immunoprecipitate KCC2 and PACSIN1, we found that the expression profiles of KCC2 and PACSIN1 are temporally aligned in the mouse brain (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on Western blot analysis of developmental expression patterns shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The addition of N-terminal KCC2b antibodies shifted a proportion of native-KCC2 to higher molecular weights in comparison to IgY control antibodies.
source: Using this approach, we first verified that the addition of N-terminal KCC2b antibodies could shift a proportion of native-KCC2 to higher molecular weights, in comparison to IgY control antibodies (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on antibody-shift assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The antibody-induced shift in native-KCC2b using N-terminal antibody also shifted a population of native-PACSIN1 to comparable higher molecular weights.
source: Next, we observed that this antibody-induced shift in native-KCC2b using N-terminal antibody also shifted a population of native-PACSIN1 to comparable higher molecular weights (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on antibody-shift assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The PACSIN family of proteins contains three members that share ~90% amino acid identity.
source: The PACSIN family of proteins contains three members that share ~90% amino acid identity (Modregger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PACSIN1 is neuron-specific and is broadly expressed across multiple brain regions.
source: PACSIN1 is neuron-specific and is broadly expressed across multiple brain regions; PACSIN2 is ubiquitous and is abundant in cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Anggono et al., 2013; Cembrowski et al., 2016), and PACSIN3 is restricted to muscle and heart (Modregger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PACSIN2 is ubiquitous and is abundant in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: PACSIN1 is neuron-specific and is broadly expressed across multiple brain regions; PACSIN2 is ubiquitous and is abundant in cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Anggono et al., 2013; Cembrowski et al., 2016), and PACSIN3 is restricted to muscle and heart (Modregger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PACSIN3 is restricted to muscle and heart.
source: PACSIN1 is neuron-specific and is broadly expressed across multiple brain regions; PACSIN2 is ubiquitous and is abundant in cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Anggono et al., 2013; Cembrowski et al., 2016), and PACSIN3 is restricted to muscle and heart (Modregger et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: KCC2 robustly associates with PACSIN1.
source: We observed that KCC2 robustly associates with PACSIN1, weakly interacts with PACSIN2, and does not interact with PACSIN3 (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in COS-7 cells shown in Figure 5e.

claim: KCC2 weakly interacts with PACSIN2.
source: We observed that KCC2 robustly associates with PACSIN1, weakly interacts with PACSIN2, and does not interact with PACSIN3 (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in COS-7 cells shown in Figure 5e.

claim: KCC2 does not interact with PACSIN3.
source: We observed that KCC2 robustly associates with PACSIN1, weakly interacts with PACSIN2, and does not interact with PACSIN3 (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments in COS-7 cells shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Mouse PACSIN1 contains a membrane-binding F-BAR domain (aa 1–325), a SH3 domain (aa 385–441), and a VAR (variable) region (aa 326–384).
source: Mouse PASCIN1 contains a membrane-binding F-BAR domain (aa 1–325), a SH3 domain (aa 385–441) that binds to phosphorylated targets, and a VAR (variable) region (aa 326–384) (Kessels and Qualmann, 2004; 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on PACSIN1 structure.

claim: Removing either the SH3 or the F-BAR region did not disrupt the KCC2:PACSIN1 interaction.
source: We discovered that removing either the SH3 (lane 3) or the F-BAR region (lane 6) did not disrupt the KCC2:PACSIN1 interaction, indicating that they are not necessary for KCC2 binding.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments with PACSIN1 deletion constructs shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Neither the SH3 domain alone nor F-BAR domain alone could interact with KCC2.
source: In an analogous result, neither the SH3 domain alone (lane 7) nor F-BAR domain alone (lane 2) could interact with KCC2.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments with PACSIN1 deletion constructs shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The VAR region of PACSIN1 is sufficient to mediate the KCC2 interaction.
source: However, KCC2 robustly co-precipitated with PACSIN1 when the VAR region alone was co-expressed with KCC2 (lane 5), indicating that the VAR region is sufficient to mediate the KCC2 interaction.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments with PACSIN1 deletion constructs shown in Figure 5f.

claim: KCC2 dysregulation has emerged as a key mechanism underlying several brain disorders including seizures, neuropathic pain, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorders (ASD).
source: KCC2 dysregulation has emerged as a key mechanism underlying several brain disorders including seizures (Fiumelli et al., 2013; Stödberg et al., 2015; Saitsu et al., 2016), neuropathic pain (Coull et al., 2003), schizophrenia (Tao et al., 2012), and autism spectrum disorders (ASD) (Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Tang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are currently no existing KCC2 enhancers approved for clinical use.
source: However, there are currently no existing KCC2 enhancers approved for clinical use, and thus there is a critical need to identify novel targets for the development of KCC2 enhancers.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of clinical therapeutics.

claim: There is a critical need to identify novel targets for the development of KCC2 enhancers.
source: However, there are currently no existing KCC2 enhancers approved for clinical use, and thus there is a critical need to identify novel targets for the development of KCC2 enhancers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of approved KCC2 enhancers and the importance of KCC2 in neurological disorders.

claim: The loss of Cl- homeostasis and thus synaptic inhibition is causal for several neurological disorders.
source: We chose to assay for the canonical KCC2 function of Cl- extrusion, as the loss of Cl- homeostasis and thus synaptic inhibition, is causal for several neurological disorders (Coull et al., 2003; Huberfeld et al., 2007; Tao et al., 2012; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Toda et al., 2014; Kahle et al., 2014; Puskarjov et al., 2014; Stödberg et al., 2015; Banerjee et al., 2016; Saitsu et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The reversal potential for GABA (EGABA) is principally determined by intracellular Cl- concentration.
source: We assayed KCC2-mediated Cl- extrusion by performing patch clamp recordings of the reversal potential for GABA (EGABA), which is principally determined by [Cl−]i (Kaila, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: When neurons expressed the PACSIN1 silencing shRNA, EGABA was significantly hyperpolarized compared to control neurons expressing the scrambled shRNA.
source: When neurons expressed the PASCIN1 silencing shRNA, EGABA was significantly hyperpolarized compared to control neurons expressing the scrambled shRNA (Figure 6a,b; control shRNA: −28.62 ± 3.07 mV, n = 9; PACSIN1 shRNA: −37.86 ± 1.73 mV, n = 11; t(18)=2.744, p=0.013).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: No significant change in GABAAR conductance was found following PACSIN1 knockdown.
source: We found no significant change in the GABAAR conductance (Figure 6a,c; control shRNA: 6.93 ± 1.32 pS, n = 9; PACSIN1 shRNA: 12.96 ± 2.71 pS, n = 11; t(18)=1.86, p=0.079), which indicates that the effect is on Cl- transport and not GABA conductance.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6a,c.

claim: No significant change in resting membrane potential (RMP) was found following PACSIN1 knockdown.
source: In addition, we found no significant change in the resting membrane potential (RMP), (Figure 6d; control shRNA: −63.41 ± 1.48 mV, n = 11; PACSIN1 shRNA: −62.77 ± 2.21 mV, n = 9; t(18)=0.246, p=0.808), which indicates the change in the driving force for Cl- was due to a change in EGABA and not RMP.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Knocking down PACSIN1 increases KCC2-mediated Cl- transporter, which results in hyperpolarized EGABA.
source: Together, these data indicate that knocking down PACSIN1 increases KCC2-mediated Cl- transporter, which results in hyperpolarized EGABA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiology data.

claim: Using gramicidin-perforated patch clamp recordings, a significant hyperpolarizing shift in EGABA was found in neurons expressing PACSIN1 shRNA versus control cells expressing scrambled shRNA.
source: Similar to our recordings above, we found a significant hyperpolarizing shift in EGABA in neurons expressing PACSIN1 shRNA versus control cells expressing scrambled shRNA (Figure 6e; control shRNA: −46.93 ± 2.78 mV, n = 7; PACSIN1 shRNA: −−72.70 ± 4.70 mV, n = 6; t(11)=4.9115, p=0.0005).
evidence: This is based on gramicidin-perforated patch clamp data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Knocking down KCC2 in cultured hippocampal neurons leads to a hyperpolarization of EGABA that strengthens inhibition, which results from an increase in KCC2-mediated Cl- extrusion.
source: Taken together, our whole-cell and gramicidin-perforated patch clamp recordings reveal that knocking down KCC2 in cultured hippocampal neurons leads to a hyperpolarization of EGABA that strengthens inhibition, which results from an increase in KCC2-mediated Cl- extrusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electrophysiology data.

claim: PACSIN1 is known to play a role as an endocytic regulatory protein.
source: Due to the known role of PACSIN1 as an endocytic regulatory protein (Anggono et al., 2006; 2013; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2006; Del Pino et al., 2014; Widagdo et al., 2016), we hypothesized that PACSIN1 negatively regulates KCC2 function by altering its expression in the surface membrane.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PACSIN1 negatively regulates KCC2 function by altering its expression in the surface membrane.
source: Due to the known role of PACSIN1 as an endocytic regulatory protein (Anggono et al., 2006; 2013; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2006; Del Pino et al., 2014; Widagdo et al., 2016), we hypothesized that PACSIN1 negatively regulates KCC2 function by altering its expression in the surface membrane.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of PACSIN1 and the experimental results.

claim: A significant increase in KCC2 fluorescence was observed in neurons expressing PACSIN1 shRNA in comparison with controls.
source: We observed a significant increase in KCC2 fluorescence in neurons expressing PASCIN1 shRNA in comparison with controls (Figure 6e; control shRNA: 58.86 ± 2.53 A.U., n = 32; PACSIN1 shRNA: 74.05 ± 2.53 A.U., n = 32; t(31)=5.272, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6e (should be 6f based on the figure).

claim: A reduction in PACSIN1 results in increased KCC2 expression and an increase in the strength of inhibition (hyperpolarization of EGABA).
source: Taken together, our electrophysiological recordings and immunofluorescence results demonstrate that a reduction in PACSIN1 results in increased KCC2 expression and an increase in the strength of inhibition (hyperpolarization of EGABA).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electrophysiology and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Overexpressing PACSIN1 produces a reduction in KCC2 expression.
source: If PACSIN1 is a bona fide negative regulator of KCC2 expression, then overexpressing PACSIN1 should produce a reduction in KCC2 expression.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis that PACSIN1 negatively regulates KCC2.

claim: A remarkable loss of KCC2 immunofluorescence was observed when PACSIN1 was overexpressed in comparison to control eGFP.
source: We observed a remarkable loss of KCC2 immunofluorescence when PACSIN1 was overexpressed in comparison to control eGFP (Figure 6f; control eGFP: 62.1 ± 2.7 A.U., n = 23; PACSIN1-eGFP: 11.31 ± 3.17 A.U., n = 16; t(37)=12.13, p<0.0001), which supports the conclusion that PACSIN1 negatively regulates KCC2 expression.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6f (should be 6g based on the figure).

claim: The mouse brain KCC2 functional interactome is comprised of 181 proteins.
source: We determined that the mouse brain KCC2 functional interactome is comprised of 181 proteins; and by mapping the KCC2 interactome to excitatory and inhibitory synapse proteomes and performing ingenuity pathway analysis, we determined that KCC2 partners are highly enriched at excitatory synapses and form a dense network with proteins involved in receptor trafficking.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: KCC2 partners are highly enriched at excitatory synapses and form a dense network with proteins involved in receptor trafficking.
source: We determined that the mouse brain KCC2 functional interactome is comprised of 181 proteins; and by mapping the KCC2 interactome to excitatory and inhibitory synapse proteomes and performing ingenuity pathway analysis, we determined that KCC2 partners are highly enriched at excitatory synapses and form a dense network with proteins involved in receptor trafficking.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the network analysis of the interactome data.

claim: PACSIN1 robustly and negatively regulates KCC2 expression.
source: Functional validation of the KCC2-PACSIN1 interaction revealed that PACSIN1 robustly and negatively regulates KCC2 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional experiments showing that PACSIN1 knockdown increases KCC2 expression and PACSIN1 overexpression decreases KCC2 expression.

claim: Ion channels and GPCRs are known to predominantly exist in large multi-protein complexes in the CNS.
source: While ion channels and GPCRs are known to predominantly exist in large multi-protein complexes in the CNS (Husi et al., 2000; Berkefeld et al., 2006; Collins et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2010; Schwenk et al., 2010; 2012; 2014; 2016; Nakamura et al., 2016; Pin and Bettler, 2016), similar studies on CNS solute carrier proteins (transporters) are still in their infancy (César-Razquin et al., 2015b; Comstra et al., 2017; Haase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Similar studies on CNS solute carrier proteins (transporters) are still in their infancy.
source: While ion channels and GPCRs are known to predominantly exist in large multi-protein complexes in the CNS (Husi et al., 2000; Berkefeld et al., 2006; Collins et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2010; Schwenk et al., 2010; 2012; 2014; 2016; Nakamura et al., 2016; Pin and Bettler, 2016), similar studies on CNS solute carrier proteins (transporters) are still in their infancy (César-Razquin et al., 2015b; Comstra et al., 2017; Haase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: SLC transporters are critical therapeutic targets in both rare and common diseases.
source: Based on the critical importance of SLC transporters as therapeutic targets in both rare and common diseases (César-Razquin et al., 2015a; Lin et al., 2015), including that of KCC2 in human neurological diseases (Blaesse et al., 2009; Medina et al., 2014), our present study also fills a general gap in the field of CNS transporter proteomics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The present study fills a general gap in the field of CNS transporter proteomics.
source: Based on the critical importance of SLC transporters as therapeutic targets in both rare and common diseases (César-Razquin et al., 2015a; Lin et al., 2015), including that of KCC2 in human neurological diseases (Blaesse et al., 2009; Medina et al., 2014), our present study also fills a general gap in the field of CNS transporter proteomics.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the study.

claim: Native-detergents C12E9 and CHAPS extract KCC2 isoforms differentially.
source: We report that native-detergents C12E9 and CHAPS extract KCC2 isoforms differentially (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Native-detergents C12E9 and CHAPS pull-down different subsets of proteins along with some common interactors.
source: We also report that native-detergents C12E9 and CHAPS pull-down different subsets of proteins along with some common interactors (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Detergent stabilities of KCC2 protein complexes are distinct.
source: This demonstrates that detergent stabilities of KCC2 protein complexes are distinct, in line with other recent ion channel proteomic studies (Müller et al., 2010; Schulte et al., 2011; Schwenk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential extraction of KCC2 complexes with different detergents, supported by citations to similar findings in other studies.

claim: The absence of previously identified KCC2 interactors in the present study may be due to weak, transient, or posttranslationally modified interactions.
source: The absence of these previously identified interactors may be due to any of the following caveats, which have been well recognized in previous ion channel and GPCR proteomic studies: (1) these interactions may be weak, transient, mediated by posttranslational modifications (Schulte et al., 2011), or mediated by intermediary partners; (2) these interactions are under-represented in the whole brain membrane fractions because they are restricted to specific brain regions; (3) antibody-epitope binding blocked endogenous interactions; (4) despite using the C12E9-based solubilization strategy that is known to stabilize ion pumps and transporters (Romero, 2009; Babu et al., 2010; Ramachandran et al., 2013) particular interactions may be better preserved by other detergent conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for missing interactors, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The absence of previously identified KCC2 interactors in the present study may be due to these interactions being under-represented in whole brain membrane fractions because they are restricted to specific brain regions.
source: The absence of these previously identified interactors may be due to any of the following caveats, which have been well recognized in previous ion channel and GPCR proteomic studies: (1) these interactions may be weak, transient, mediated by posttranslational modifications (Schulte et al., 2011), or mediated by intermediary partners; (2) these interactions are under-represented in the whole brain membrane fractions because they are restricted to specific brain regions; (3) antibody-epitope binding blocked endogenous interactions; (4) despite using the C12E9-based solubilization strategy that is known to stabilize ion pumps and transporters (Romero, 2009; Babu et al., 2010; Ramachandran et al., 2013) particular interactions may be better preserved by other detergent conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for missing interactors.

source: The absence of these previously identified interactors may be due to any of the following caveats, which have been well recognized in previous ion channel and GPCR proteomic studies: (1) these interactions may be weak, transient, mediated by posttranslational modifications (Schulte et al., 2011), or mediated by intermediary partners; (2) these interactions are under-represented in the whole brain membrane fractions because they are restricted to specific brain regions; (3) antibody-epitope binding blocked endogenous interactions; (4) despite using the C12E9-based solubilization strategy that is known to stabilize ion pumps and transporters (Romero, 2009; Babu et al., 2010; Ramachandran et al., 2013) particular interactions may be better preserved by other detergent conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for missing interactors.

claim: Particular KCC2 interactions may be better preserved by other detergent conditions.
source: The absence of these previously identified interactors may be due to any of the following caveats, which have been well recognized in previous ion channel and GPCR proteomic studies: (1) these interactions may be weak, transient, mediated by posttranslational modifications (Schulte et al., 2011), or mediated by intermediary partners; (2) these interactions are under-represented in the whole brain membrane fractions because they are restricted to specific brain regions; (3) antibody-epitope binding blocked endogenous interactions; (4) despite using the C12E9-based solubilization strategy that is known to stabilize ion pumps and transporters (Romero, 2009; Babu et al., 2010; Ramachandran et al., 2013) particular interactions may be better preserved by other detergent conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for missing interactors, with citations supporting the use of C12E9.

claim: Single particle tracking of surface KCC2 has revealed that ~66% of KCC2 is located synaptically.
source: Single particle tracking of surface KCC2 has revealed that ~ 66% of KCC2 is located synaptically (Chamma et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The density of surface KCC2 was not reportedly different between excitatory and inhibitory synapses.

evidence: This is based on previous research on KCC2 localization.

claim: KCC2 was shown to dwell longer at excitatory synapses.
source: While the density of surface KCC2 was not reportedly different between excitatory and inhibitory synapses, KCC2 was shown to dwell longer at excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is based on previous research on KCC2 localization.

claim: The observation that KCC2 interacting proteins are primarily enriched at excitatory synapses is in line with the increased confinement of KCC2 at excitatory synapses.
source: Our observation that KCC2 interacting proteins are primarily enriched at excitatory synapses in comparison to inhibitory synapses is in line with this increased confinement of KCC2 at excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the interactome data to previous findings on KCC2 localization.

claim: Our knowledge of the proteins present at inhibitory synapses is incomplete.
source: One potential answer to both these questions is that: because of the difficulty in identifying components of inhibitory synapses, our knowledge of the proteins present at these structures is incomplete.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: KCC2 itself was not identified in any of the inhibitory synapse-enriched proteomes used for network mapping.
source: In this context, it is interesting to note that KCC2 itself was not identified in any of the above inhibitory synapse-enriched proteomes, and we assigned KCC2 as a member of the inhibitory synapse during network analyses, because of its established function at this locus.
evidence: This is an observation about the absence of KCC2 in published inhibitory synapse proteomes.

claim: KCC2 may 'moon-light' between inhibitory and excitatory synapses.
source: Another possibility is that KCC2 'moon-lights' between inhibitory and excitatory synapses, as previously suggested (Blaesse and Schmidt, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to previous speculation.

claim: 29 proteins (excluding KCC2) in the interactome are enriched at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Our interactome supports this hypothesis as we identified 29 proteins (excluding KCC2) that are enriched at both synapses.
evidence: This is based on the network mapping analysis of the interactome data.

claim: Emerging evidence from cortex suggests that excitatory and inhibitory synapses may not be strictly distinct structures.
source: While the notion that excitatory and inhibitory synapses are distinct structures is widely accepted, emerging evidence from cortex suggests this may not be strictly true (Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Under circumstances where excitatory and inhibitory synapses are in close physical proximity, the molecular complex involving KCC2 and moonlighting proteins are ideally placed to execute cell-intrinsic E/I balance regulation.
source: Under circumstances where excitatory and inhibitory synapses are in close physical proximity, the molecular complex involving KCC2 and these moonlighting proteins are ideally placed to execute cell-intrinsic E/I balance regulation, a hypothesis stemming from our present study that requires rigorous experimental testing.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the interactome data and previous findings on synapse proximity.

claim: 4.1N is a critical mediator of KCC2's non-canonical transporter-independent function in regulating dendritic spine structures.
source: Ever since the first discovery that KCC2 participates in the regulation of dendritic spine structures (Li et al., 2007), several studies have demonstrated 4.1N as a critical mediator of this non-canonical transporter-independent KCC2 function (Horn et al., 2010; Gauvain et al., 2011; Chamma et al., 2013; Fiumelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: COFL1 and ARHGEF7 (Beta-pix) have been identified to interact with KCC2 and are involved in KCC2's non-canonical function.
source: Recently however, additional molecular players underlying this phenomenon, including COFL1, and ARHGEF7 (Beta-pix) have been identified to interact with KCC2 (Chevy et al., 2015; Llano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The present study identifies diverse high confidence cytoskeletal organizers (CRMPs, 14-3-3 isoforms, SRCIN1, VCP, KIF21B) previously unsuspected to mediate KCC2-dependent non-canonical function.
source: In the present study, we identify diverse high confidence (Platinum, Gold) cytoskeletal organizers belonging to distinct protein families such as CRMPs, 14-3-3 isoforms, SRCIN1, VCP, KIF21B, previously unsuspected to mediate KCC2-dependant non-canonical function.
evidence: This is based on the identification of these proteins in the interactome.

claim: PACSIN1 is a well-established endocytic adapter protein that regulates the surface expression of distinct glutamate and glycine receptors.
source: PACSIN1 is a well-established endocytic adapter protein that regulates the surface expression of distinct glutamate (Anggono et al., 2006, 2013; Pérez-Otaño et al., 2006; Widagdo et al., 2016) and glycine receptors (Del Pino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Native-KCC2 assembles as a hetero-oligomer that migrates predominantly above ~400 kDa.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Native-PACSIN1 also migrates above ~400 kDa.
source: Similar to KCC2, native-PACSIN1 also migrates above ~400 kDa (Kessels and Qualmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: SLC12A5 and PACSIN1 mRNA transcripts increase in parallel in multiple brain regions throughout development.
source: Here, we report that while SLC12A5 and PACSIN1 mRNA transcripts increase in parallel in multiple brain regions throughout development, PACSIN1 overexpression remarkably decreases total KCC2 abundance.
evidence: This is based on transcriptomic analysis presented in the study.

claim: PACSIN1 overexpression remarkably decreases total KCC2 abundance.
source: Here, we report that while SLC12A5 and PACSIN1 mRNA transcripts increase in parallel in multiple brain regions throughout development, PACSIN1 overexpression remarkably decreases total KCC2 abundance.
evidence: This is based on the immunofluorescence data showing decreased KCC2 with PACSIN1 overexpression.

claim: KCC2 and PACSIN1 are both dynamically regulated by phosphorylation and PKC.
source: Since KCC2 and PACSIN1 are both dynamically regulated by phosphorylation and PKC (Anggono et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2007; Clayton et al., 2009; Kahle et al., 2013), we predict that upon KCC2 phosphorylation, PACSIN1 uncouples from KCC2 rendering it incapable of negatively regulating KCC2.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PACSIN1 shRNA increases KCC2 expression and strengthens inhibition.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that PACSIN1 shRNA increases KCC2 expression and strengthens inhibition, indicating that PACSIN1 is a target for intervention to upregulate KCC2 during pathological states.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from electrophysiology and immunofluorescence.

source: In conclusion, the KCC2 interactome as presented here, serves as a molecular framework for systematically exploring how KCC2 up and down states can be dynamically regulated by its native molecular constituents, thereby providing a blueprint for subsequent detailed functional investigations.
